A few things worth flagging up front, since they'll change how you scope the checklist:

**On terminology.** It's the CPRA (California Privacy Rights Act, Prop 24, 2020), not CCPR. It amended the CCPA rather than replacing it, so the operative citation is still the CCPA at Civil Code 1798.100 et seq. The regulator is the California Privacy Protection Agency, which now brands itself CalPrivacy — you'll see both names in sources.

**Your starting point has moved.** The bigger development is the regulations package approved by the Office of Administrative Law on September 22, 2025, effective January 1, 2026. That shifts the CCPA from a disclosure regime to an operational one: documented risk assessments beginning January 1, 2026, reviewed at least every three years and updated within 45 days of a material change; independent annual cybersecurity audits on a revenue-based glide path — April 1, 2028 for businesses over $100 million, 2029 for $50–100 million, 2030 for under $50 million; and ADMT compliance by January 1, 2027. A readiness assessment built only around privacy-policy and DSAR mechanics is now roughly half the picture.

**Three sources do most of the work.** cppa.ca.gov/regulations for the controlling text, leginfo.legislature.ca.gov to confirm code placement for the 2025-session bills, and oag.ca.gov/privacy for enforcement posture. **The nearest deadline isn't a CCPA one.** Beginning August 1, 2026, data brokers must access DROP at least once every 45 days to retrieve and process deletion requests, and the Delete Act's data broker definition has no explicit business-size threshold — businesses outside CCPA scope can still be caught. ## The escalation ladder you've accidentally built

Part 1 needs nothing from the client but permission — it's all externally observable. Part 2 requires interviews, document access, and executive time. Part 3 is forward-looking and never really finishes. That maps almost exactly onto a lead magnet → paid engagement → retainer funnel. I'd lean into that deliberately rather than pricing all three as equivalent deliverables.

The one thing that will make or break the set: give all three a shared spine. Every finding in Part 1 should carry the same control ID it has in Part 2 and the same ID in the Part 3 roadmap. Otherwise you produce three documents that read like they came from three different firms. The workbook already uses stable IDs — extend that into a single control register and have all three deliverables render from it.

## Part 1 — Website assessment

This is your strongest product because it's evidence-based and repeatable. Structure it around what you can prove with a screenshot and a timestamp:

- Notice at collection — present at or before the point of collection, on every collection surface, not just the homepage
- Privacy policy content requirements — categories collected, sources, purposes, disclosure recipients, retention periods, rights, updated within twelve months
- Opt-out mechanics — "Do Not Sell or Share," "Limit the Use of My Sensitive Personal Information," and the symmetry rule: opting out cannot take more steps than opting in
- **Global Privacy Control honoring** — test it. Send the signal, then check whether the opt-out actually registers and whether third-party tags stop firing. This is objectively testable, it's been a documented enforcement focus, and most sites fail it. It's the single most compelling finding you can put in front of a prospect.
- Pre-consent tracker inventory — what fires before any interaction, and where the data goes
- Dark pattern review against the regulations' consent standards
- Minors, financial incentive notices, and authorized agent handling where relevant

Two cautions. Keep the methodology strictly observational — behave like a visitor, get written authorization before you scan anything, and say so in the report. And separate the CIPA exposure into its own clearly-labelled section: pixel and session-replay findings are litigation risk rather than regulatory risk, and clients react very differently to "you may be sued next quarter" than to "the agency may notice."

## Part 2 — Organizational posture

The mistake to avoid here is organizing by statute. Clients can't act on a document structured around Civil Code sections. Organize by data lifecycle and let the citations sit in a mapping column:

inventory and mapping → collection and notice → rights operations → vendor and contract management → security → retention and deletion → risk assessment and ADMT governance → incident response → training and accountability.

Put an applicability decision tree at the very front. Revenue band, consumer volume, sensitive PI volume, data broker status, ADMT usage. That gate determines which sections apply *and* which deadline tier the client sits in — and it's what lets you tell a $60M-revenue client that their first cybersecurity audit certification is due April 1, 2029 covering calendar 2028, so evidence collection starts in about eighteen months. That runway framing is the whole value of Part 2.

Score against evidence, not self-attestation. A five-point scale with hard anchors works well: documented / approved / operationalized / measured / independently verified. Ask for the artifact at each level. A client who says "yes we have a retention schedule" and cannot produce it scores a 1, and that gap *is* the finding.

Budget for interviews across legal, marketing and adtech, IT and security, HR, procurement, and analytics. Marketing is usually where the undisclosed data flows live, and they're rarely in the room when privacy gets discussed.

## Part 3 — Enhancements

This is the one most likely to drift into filler. Anchor it to something external and re-testable, or it reads as opinion.

I'd use the NIST Privacy Framework as the spine and express the whole thing as a sequenced roadmap — 30 day, 90 day, six month, twelve month — with an owner, effort estimate, and dependency for every item. Not a list of good ideas. A plan someone can put in a budget request.

Content worth including: multistate deltas with California as the strictest baseline and other states as exceptions; AI and ADMT governance ahead of the January 2027 date; universal opt-out signal readiness ahead of AB 566; privacy-by-design gates in the development lifecycle; and data minimization framed as storage and breach-exposure cost reduction rather than compliance. That last framing gets budget approved when compliance framing doesn't.

Part 3 is also your natural retainer: annual reassessment, quarterly regulatory delta briefings, re-scoring against the same control register so the client can see movement.

## Two cross-cutting things

**Date-stamp every finding.** Put "assessed against California law as of [date]" on the cover of all three. The regulatory picture is moving fast enough that a report without an as-of date becomes a liability within a year.

**Be deliberate about the legal-advice line.** If you're not practising as a California attorney, the deliverables should describe compliance *readiness* and observable *gaps*, and route legal conclusions to counsel. This isn't just a disclaimer question — it changes how you phrase findings. "Your privacy policy does not disclose retention periods for the categories listed in Section 3" is an observation. "You are in violation of §1798.130" is a legal conclusion. The first is more useful to the client anyway, and it's what makes a lawyer comfortable referring work to you rather than seeing you as a competitor. That referral channel is probably your best client acquisition path in this market.
